title: Machines and computation histories

based_on.title: Computability and Incompleteness
based_on.pages: 35–41 (§2.6, machine equivalence, primitive-recursive histories and search; version 2007-01-09)

based_on.title: Formalizing Computability Theory via Partial Recursive Functions
based_on.pages: 12:9–12:13 (§§4.2–5.2, paired recursive programs and resource-bounded evaluation; ITP 2019)

summary: Record a computation as numbered states, check its finite history, and prove that one search for such a history computes every partial recursive function.
abstract: Start one counter at the input and another at zero, then decrease the first by one and increase the second by two until the first reaches zero. The second counter holds twice the input, and the successive counter pairs form a finite record that can be checked one transition at a time. An arithmetic machine stores its state as a natural number and uses primitive-recursive routines to initialize it, update it, test for stopping and read its output. Each transition may perform a whole bounded calculation. These machines compute exactly the partial recursive functions, and their successful finite records can be checked by primitive-recursive tests. Consequently, any partial recursive computation can be organized as one unbounded search for a successful record followed by extraction of its output, even when its original description uses nested searches.
